findings.suggestion: how much
findings.reason: For the intended everyday price question, how much is the familiar reusable phrase. What price is understandable and not inherently ungrammatical, but less useful as the default spoken shop question. Retain the price sense rather than expanding the concept to all quantities.

findings.suggestion: Keep board; specify classroom board in meaning/context
findings.reason: Board is a common A1 classroom expression in Cambridge, so replacement solely for being short is unwarranted. Other forms specify a school board (Japanese specifically blackboard); clarify that sense rather than implying every board is a blackboard.

findings.suggestion: Keep break; identify school break in meaning/context
findings.reason: School vocabulary supplies context, but isolated break is also a verb and a broader rest period. Latvian starpbrīdis and Russian перемена point specifically to the gap between lessons. A context note is sufficient; no full sentence required.

findings.suggestion: Keep seller for a person selling; use shop assistant only if the concept is explicitly shop staff
findings.reason: Seller is a normal learner word, not an error. The Japanese form 販売員 specifically suggests sales staff. Cambridge distinguishes a general seller from a shop sales assistant; establish the intended person before narrowing the English word.

findings.suggestion: Keep palm; identify palm of hand in meaning/context
findings.reason: The body block makes the hand sense plausible, but a standalone prompt also names a tree. Cambridge explicitly separates these senses. Do not replace palm with hand: that would change the protected meaning.

findings.suggestion: Keep leg; disambiguate the source sense and review foot distractor vocab-0135
findings.reason: English leg and foot are distinct common terms, but current Russian нога can denote the limb or foot. In RU→EN, foot is an actual distractor beside leg; this needs a bilingual sense check. Japanese 足 also commonly spans foot/leg, although Japanese is target-only. English dictionary evidence supports the distinction; the cross-language overlap is model editorial.

findings.suggestion: Keep stomach; record belly/body area as the intended everyday sense
findings.reason: Latvian vēders, Russian живот and Japanese お腹 denote the belly/abdominal area. English stomach also legitimately has this ordinary external-body sense, as Cambridge confirms; it need not be replaced with the technical abdomen. Avoid teaching it as an exact anatomical organ equivalence.

findings.suggestion: Keep UK plaster; replace bandage distractor vocab-0149 or explicitly constrain the variety/sense
findings.reason: Plaster is legitimate common British English for the small adhesive dressing. Cambridge also records US bandage as a Band-Aid, so bandage is a defensible English answer to Russian пластырь / Latvian plāksteris in the current reverse question. Solve the answer collision without treating either national variety as incorrect.

findings.suggestion: Keep footwear for the general category; consider shoes only after a meaning decision
findings.reason: Footwear accurately includes shoes, boots and other foot coverings, matching the current broad category. Shoes may be the more immediately useful spoken request, but replacing footwear with shoes silently narrows the concept. No measured comparative frequency claim is made.

findings.suggestion: Keep pot for the deep cooking vessel; clarify pan vocab-0210 as frying pan
findings.reason: Actual distractor vocab-0210 is pan. Cambridge defines pan broadly and even explains pots and pans as different types of pan. In LV/RU→EN, pan can name the cooking vessel intended by katls/кастрюля. The English answer set needs a narrower frying-pan label.

findings.suggestion: frying pan
findings.reason: Current panna / сковорода / フライパン specifies a shallow frying pan, whereas English pan includes deeper vessels and baking tins. Frying pan is a short familiar compound that preserves the exact sense and resolves the collision in vocab-0209; US skillet remains legitimate but adds an unnecessary alternative.

findings.suggestion: Keep pepper with vegetable context, or use sweet pepper if a standalone cue is needed
findings.reason: Pepper is valid ordinary English for the vegetable, but also the seasoning. Current paprika / сладкий перец / ピーマン means the vegetable. Cambridge records sweet pepper and US bell pepper as alternatives. Clarify this useful sense rather than replacing a correct British use simply with a US variant.

findings.suggestion: chicken, with food sense retained in concept metadata
findings.reason: Chicken meat is understandable and safely explicit; ordinary English already uses chicken for the meat, as Cambridge definitions and food examples show. Optional shortening improves the default without creating a new synonym. Keep vocab-0368 hen as the animal concept and recheck bindings before any later change.

findings.suggestion: Keep lunch; review dinner distractor vocab-0252 for reverse directions
findings.reason: Dinner is an actual distractor to lunch. Cambridge says dinner is the main meal, sometimes at midday in Britain and also records this in American English. Russian обед / Latvian pusdienas may refer to that midday main meal. Do not mark regional dinner use wrong; narrow context or change the distractor after bilingual review.

findings.suggestion: Keep dinner for evening meal; record the intended meal time
findings.reason: Dinner is a normal beginner term, not an error, but not universally synonymous with evening meal. Current vakariņas / ужин / 夕食 specifically means evening meal. Context matters, especially because this entry is a distractor to lunch in vocab-0251.

findings.suggestion: paintbrush
findings.reason: Current ota and the art context identify a painting brush; Russian кисть and Japanese 筆 also fit that purpose. English brush includes hair and cleaning brushes. Paintbrush is one short familiar compound that makes the intended tool clearer; the current form is understandable in its art block.

findings.suggestion: letter of the alphabet, or retain letter with an alphabet context cue
findings.reason: English letter commonly means a posted message as well as an alphabet symbol. Latvian burts and Russian буква specify the symbol; Japanese 文字 is the broader written character. Keep the symbol sense explicit. The four-word clarification fits the short-item policy but is a proposal, not an active edit.

findings.suggestion: Keep English word; review Japanese phrase distractor vocab-0403
findings.reason: In EN→JA the actual choices include 単語 as correct and 語句 for phrase as a distractor. 語句 can cover words as well as phrases, so word may have two defensible answers. English word and phrase are ordinary distinct teaching concepts; Japanese bilingual verification is required. Do not replace the English with a novel synonym to work around the issue.

findings.suggestion: Keep look at; provide a concrete visual context or review watch distractor vocab-0433
findings.reason: Look at directs the eyes; watch is looking over time, especially at something moving. The actual answer set includes to watch / vērot / наблюдать / 観る. Without an object or duration, broad meanings overlap in some situations. This is a context-sensitive risk for bilingual review rather than proof that every question has two correct answers.

findings.suggestion: Keep to search; consider to look for only if a simpler everyday phrase is preferred
findings.reason: To search is valid learner vocabulary and matches trying to find something. For the broad meklēt / искать / 探す sense, to look for is an optional everyday alternative, not a required correction or an extra synonym to add. Existing taught look at is a different pattern; do not conflate them.

notes: Inspected all 510 records in dist/audit-input.json, including English form, concept meaning, all other-language forms and the three actual distractor IDs/forms per record. This is an English-focused model editorial audit, not independent certification of Latvian, Russian or Japanese. Findings on cross-language ambiguity identify review risks; fluent bilingual adjudication remains pending.

Unflagged entries are working keep decisions only. They are not native-speaker approval, measured learner outcomes or certification of every possible sense/register. Ordinary nouns, infinitive vocabulary forms and understandable fragments are valid learning items; no blanket requirement for full sentences was applied.

Legitimate British and American usage was retained, including shop, toilet, trousers, neighbour, autumn, pavement, centre, grey, plaster, yogurt and eraser. No replacement was proposed just to standardize national variety. Hen, trolleybus and porridge were retained for their precise meanings/local usefulness; unusualness in one region alone is not an error.

Cambridge learner dictionary pages cited in findings were read on 2026-11-23. Source-supported means the cited dictionary supports the lexical distinction or usage evidence, not that it has approved this course or the proposed edit. Suggestions and priorities remain editorial judgments. Cross-language claims not established by these English sources are labelled model-editorial.

Beginner framework consulted: https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/about/wordlists/oxford3000-5000 . Oxford describes frequency plus learner relevance and CEFR guidance across A1–B2, not a ranked survival list. Cambridge marks senses independently (for example board classroom A1, chicken A2, pan/frying pan B1, palm hand C2). Such labels are guidance, not a reason to remove a useful concept, nor evidence for an invented frequency ranking of these 510 items.

No active vocabulary, meaning, binding, distractor, guide, audio, app, task-list or publication change is implemented by this research file. Where a short English alternative is suggested, preserve the concept and check all directions plus audio/guides before any separately authorized correction.
